# The Number

My mother has been dead for four years, and every month I pay the phone company forty-five dollars to keep her alive a little longer.

Autopay. I set it up the week after the funeral, when I found out the number would be released after ninety days of inactivity. Released, like an animal, like a bird. Somewhere out there her number would be handed to a stranger, and some stranger's mother would answer when I called, and I could not allow that. So now the phone company has a standing arrangement with me: forty-five dollars a month, and in exchange her number sits in their servers like a held breath, assigned to nobody, waiting.

Her greeting was nothing special. That's what I loved about it. "Hey, it's Ellen—leave it after the beep." Flat, a little rushed, the way she talked when she was doing something else, which was always. You can hear a cabinet close near the end. You can hear, very faintly, my father asking her a question from another room, six years before he died.

Some nights I call it. Not all nights. I scroll to E, thumb over the green, and usually that's enough—just to see it there, the same number I dialed when I was seven, stretching the kitchen cord down the hall and around the bathroom door for privacy. She ported the house line to a cell phone at sixty-eight because my brother nagged her into it, so the number in my phone and the number in my body are the same number. I know it the way I know my own hands.

Her voicemails were never about anything. "It's me. I made too much soup. Come by Sunday, or don't, but there's soup." She never said goodbye. She'd get to the end of a thought and just—hang up, mid-breath, like the machine couldn't hold her attention one second longer. For years I found this rude. Now I would give anything to be dismissed by her again.

The last message is eleven seconds long. I have it backed up three times, on drives and in the cloud, in a file called mom—final.mp3, which is a terrible name but there it is. It's from a Tuesday in October, three days before the end. "Call me back. A pigeon's been coming to my fire escape and I think it likes me. That's all. Call me back." I did call back. I know I called back. But I couldn't tell you now what we said, and I never asked about the pigeon—not enough, not the right questions—and so the pigeon is hers. It's the one thing she took with her.

Here is what I did not know: the greeting was not mine. The messages were not mine. When you pay for a dead woman's number, you are renting a room in the phone company's building, and when you stop, they don't just reassign the number. They clear the room. Wipe the box. Everything I'd saved—the pigeon, the soup, my father's voice in the background of a greeting recorded in 2009—all of it lived on their servers, not in my phone. I never recorded the greeting. I kept meaning to. I thought the servers were forever, and that forever owed me something.

The card on file expired in February and I didn't notice the emails. In March, on a Tuesday night, because I'd had a good day and wanted to end it with her, I called, and a man's voice said, "You reached Des. You know what to do."

I sat down on the kitchen floor. Des. A young voice, unhurried, faintly amused—a man who has never once thought about his own mortality. His friends are in her voicemail box now. They leave messages about parties. I called every night that week just to hear the shape of it, the way you drive past your old house and stare at strangers' curtains.

I want to tell you I did something dignified. I didn't. I called and, after his beep, said: *I'm sorry to do this to you. That number was my mother's for thirty-one years. She died four years ago and I kept paying for it so I could hear her say leave it after the beep. I don't need anything from you. Just—be nice to it.* Then I hung up before he could ever hear me, which is not how it works, which means I hung up on myself.

Des never called back. He didn't have to. There was nothing to say.

Here is what I have instead. I have eleven seconds of pigeon. I have her syntax, which turns out to be unkillable. I start all my messages with *it's me*, as if there were only one me in the world, as if the person on the other end couldn't possibly have caller ID, as if the phone were still a bell ringing in an empty house and the voice on the line a mystery, a stranger calling out of the dark wanting to be found. I hang up without goodbyes. My brother says I've started doing the thing where I get to the end of a thought and just—

And Des's beep, back when I still called, was the same beep. Beeps are universal. Some nights that was almost enough.

Last Sunday I made too much soup. I stood in my kitchen with a pot the size of a bathtub and understood, finally, what she had been doing all those years—not cooking, signaling. Reaching for the one excuse that never runs out. I called my sister, and when she answered I said: It's me. I made too much soup. Come by, or don't.

But there's soup.

The prompt is wide open: 1000 words, write whatever comes. This is a creative writing invitation. The best response is probably something genuinely interesting—not a filler essay, not a lecture, but something that feels alive. Free writing, but with craft. Let me think about what would be worth reading.

Options:
1. A short story — complete narrative arc in 1000 words (flash fiction). Classic and satisfying.
2. A personal essay / meditation on something — could be about writing itself, memory, time.
3. A prose poem or lyrical fragment.
4. Something meta about the prompt itself ("write whatever comes to you") — that could be clever but risks being precious.
5. A hybrid: a story that begins from the premise of the prompt.

The most generous and impressive thing is probably a piece of flash fiction that actually earns its 1000 words—something with emotional weight, a turn, specificity. Or a lyrical essay that moves. Let me try to write something with real texture.

Let me brainstorm story seeds:

- A locksmith who can open anything but his daughter's diary. Interesting tension, small and human.
- The last day of a laundromat before it closes. People intersect.
- Someone who inherits a voicemail box—keeps calling a dead person's number to hear their greeting.
- A translator translating a letter and discovering it's from their own parent.
- A woman who works at a lost-and-found and the objects people never claim.
- An old man teaching his granddaughter to whistle so the dog comes home.
- A night-shift radio host taking calls from insomniacs, and one call that changes things.
- The moment before someone says something they can't take back.
- A story about the moon drifting slightly closer each year and nobody acknowledging it—magical realism.
- Two strangers on a bench, one is leaving the city forever.

I like the voicemail one—grief, technology, specificity. Or the lost-and-found. Or the locksmith. Let me think about which gives the richest 1000 words.

The voicemail idea: A person keeps their dead mother's phone number alive, calling it just to hear "You've reached Ruth, leave a message." Then one day the greeting changes—someone else has the number now. That's a gut-punch with a natural arc: setup, ritual, disruption, turn. The turn could be: they leave a message anyway, for the stranger. Or the stranger calls back. Or—better—the protagonist eventually lets the number go, and the final beat is what they keep instead. There's room for texture: what the mother's voice said, the details of her, the mechanics of paying for a dead line, the guilt of it.

Actually, a well-known real phenomenon: people keeping dead loved ones' numbers, Apple once planned to delete voicemails from dead people and people protested. I can write this without referencing that.

Structure for ~1000 words:
1. Open with the ritual—calling the number at night, what the greeting sounds like, the specific music her daughter picked or the voice itself. Establish that mother has been dead X years, that the protagonist pays the phone company monthly.
2. Backstory braided in: mother's life, small details—the way she said the protagonist's name, her habit of leaving voicemails that started mid-thought, the last voicemail that still exists and is saved.
3. The disruption: one night the greeting is different—a man's voice, or a generic robotic one. The number has been recycled.
4. Protagonist's reaction: calls the number repeatedly, anger, absurdity of grieving a phone number. Maybe calls the actual new owner? That could be a scene: they call and a stranger answers—awkward, could hang up. Or leave a message telling the stranger about who had the number.
5. Turn/resolution: what remains. The saved voicemail, played so often it's worn. Maybe the realization that the number was never her—she's elsewhere: in the protagonist's own habit of leaving long voicemails, in her hands, etc. End with an image, not a moral.

Actually maybe the ending: the protagonist dials the old number one last time and when the stranger's greeting plays, says nothing—or says "wrong number," softly, and that phrase carries double meaning. Or: they finally delete... no, keep the saved voicemail. Maybe end with them recording their own outgoing greeting and realizing their voice sounds like hers. That's a nice closing image: inheritance in the voice.

Let me think about voice and details. First person feels right for intimacy. Narrator: a daughter, mid-thirties maybe. Mother: Ruth? Marie? Let's pick something warm but not saccharine—"Dolores"? "Ellen"? I'll go with something like "her voice, when it answered..." Maybe don't overname. Actually naming helps: "My mother's number was 718-something." Brooklyn area code 718 gives place. She could have had the number for 40 years—the same number since the narrator was a child. That's a detail people relate to: the family landline number you could dial from memory even now, your hand remembering the pattern.

Hybrid: it was a cell phone by the end. The greeting: "Hi, you've reached Ellen. Leave it after the beep." Something casual, hers.

The ritual: every couple weeks, sometimes drunk, sometimes sober, the narrator calls, lets it ring twice—no, lets it go to voicemail, listens to the greeting, hangs up. Never leaves a message. The monthly $45 to keep the line is described frankly.

Details of the mother: she left voicemails that were really just her thinking out loud—"It's me. I made too much soup. That's all, I just—anyway." She said the narrator's childhood nickname. The last voicemail: three days before she died, something mundane—"Call me back, I want to tell you about the pigeon"—and the pigeon story died with her, which is a wonderful ache. The narrator has never learned what the pigeon did. That's a strong concrete mystery to hang the piece on.

The disruption: one night the greeting is gone. A stranger's voice, or the robotic "The subscriber you have dialed..." Better: a young man's voice: "You reached Marco. Leave it." The violence of that casualness.

Then: the narrator, absurdly, one night dials and when Marco's beep comes, leaves a message—explaining nothing, or explaining everything: "I don't know why I'm telling you this..." Maybe: "That was my mother's number for thirty-one years." And then—the turn—Marco calls back? Risky, could be too neat. Alternative: Marco texts back a screenshot? Too neat. Maybe: silence, and that's fine—the narrator didn't want an answer, just wanted the number to know. Then final movement: the narrator plays the saved last voicemail; the pigeon; decides not to delete; notices her own greeting on her own phone—if she could hear herself she'd hear her mother. Maybe she calls her own phone to test it and there in her own voice is the mother's cadence—"Leave it after the beep"—and that's the inheritance.

Ending line possibilities: "I let it ring." Or: "The pigeon, I decided, could keep its secret. Some things my mother got to take with her." Something like: "Somewhere in the city a stranger was getting my mother's calls now, collecting her wrong numbers, her telemarketers, her old friends. I hoped he'd be kind to them." That's lovely—hoping the stranger is kind to the incoming calls. Could use that.

Word budget ~1000. Let me draft with attention to rhythm. I should aim for roughly 950–1050 words. The user said "you have 1000 words," so hitting close to 1000 honors the constraint. I don't need to count exactly but should be in the neighborhood—substantial but not bloated. Let me write it well.

Draft:

Title? Maybe "The Number" or "Eight Six Zero Two" (last four digits). A title like "Leave It After the Beep" could be nice. Or no title. A title adds polish. "The Last Four Digits"? I'll go with something simple: "The Number."

Opening: "My mother has been dead for four years, and every month I pay the phone company forty-five dollars to keep her alive a little longer." Strong opening—paradox up front.

Then the mechanics: autopay, the line, the greeting. "You've got Ellen—leave it after the beep." Wait—should the mother's greeting be described precisely? Yes: "Hey, it's Ellen. Leave it after the beep." The narrator describes the flatness of it, recorded in 2009 or so, the kitchen sounds, the dog bark in the background.

Ritual paragraph: some nights, after dinner, she dials. Doesn't press call immediately—holds the number, thumb hovering. Sometimes just looking at it is enough. The physics of it: her mother's phone probably in a landfill somewhere, but the number lives in the company's computers, assigned to nobody, waiting.

Backstory: the number followed her from the landline? Actually simpler: mother got a cell late, in her sixties, kept the same number the whole family knew. Or the number was originally the house line ported to the cell—"She ported the house number when she finally got a cell phone at sixty-eight, so the number I dialed at seven years old, stretching the cord into the bathroom for privacy, is the same one in my phone now." Good detail—phone cords stretched into closets.

Voicemail details: mother's messages were never to the point. "It's me. I made too much kapushta—" maybe not a specific ethnic dish unless I set heritage; keep it "soup." "It's me. I made too much soup again. Come by Sunday, or don't, but there's soup." Her habit of not saying goodbye, just hanging up mid-breath.

The last voicemail: saved. "Tuesday. Three days before. 'Call me back. A pigeon's been coming to my fire escape and I think it likes me. That's all. Call me back.'" And: "I never called back. Or I did and I don't remember what she said, which is worse." Actually stronger: "I did call back. But I never asked enough about the pigeon, and now the pigeon is hers forever—the one thing she took with her." Something like that. Or the narrator can't remember whether she called back at all—that's more honest and more painful: memory decay around the edges.

The disruption scene: a Tuesday night in March (specificity), she dials, and instead of her mother: "a man's voice, young, unhurried: 'You reached Des. You know what to do.'" The narrator's physical reaction: sat on the kitchen floor. The number reassigned—the company held it the legal minimum (90 days? actually numbers typically get recycled eventually; I'll keep vague—"the way the law allows") and gave it away.

Reaction: she called every night that week just to hear Des. Learned his cadence. Hated him. Hated that his friends' voices were in her mother's voicemail box now—no wait, the old messages are gone? That's a question: when a number is reassigned, the voicemail box is wiped. So the last voicemail—the pigeon—was it saved? If the narrator saved it (voicemails saved on the phone company's server), it died with the reassignment. Oh—that's the knife: the greeting was one thing, but the pigeon voicemail lived in the carrier's mailbox, and now Des's messages live there instead. So the narrator lost the greeting and the last message at once. That raises the stakes of the disruption. But maybe she'd have saved it to her own phone/digitally—careful narrators do. I could say: "I had it backed up, of course. A file called Mom—voicemail.mp3. It's on three drives and in the cloud. It survived. But the box where it lived is his now." Good—acknowledges modern reality while keeping the loss.

Then the message she leaves Des: one night, after his beep, she says: "I'm sorry to do this to you. That number was my mother's for thirty-one years. She died four years ago and I kept paying for it so I could hear her say leave it after the beep. You have her number now. I don't need anything. Just—be nice to it." Then hangs up before the beep cuts her off—no, you speak after the beep. She leaves it. Des never calls back. Maybe he does something small: nothing. Silence is right.

Turn: what she keeps. Describes playing the pigeon file. "It's eleven seconds long." The mundane miracle of it. Then the inheritance: she notices her own outgoing message—or her sister says so, or she hears herself leaving messages for friends: "It's me" as an opening, hanging up without goodbye. "I start most of my messages with 'It's me,' as if there were only one me, as if the person on the other end couldn't possibly have caller ID, as if the phone were still the magical bell it was when we were girls and the voice on the tape a stranger's voice, any voice, someone calling out of the dark wanting to be found."

Ending: the final beat. Options: (a) She dials the old number one last time—maybe she still does, sometimes, and when Des's beep comes, she just listens and hangs up, and it's almost the same. "Des's beep is the same beep. Beeps are universal. Some nights that's enough." (b) The hope that Des is kind to her mother's calls. (c) The soup: she makes too much soup now. Oh—(c) is good: the inheritance of "I made too much soup." Ending line: "Last Sunday I made too much soup. I called my sister and said, It's me. I made too much soup. Come by, or don't. But there's soup." That's a beautiful close—grief metabolized into continuation, the mother's syntax living in her mouth. Could combine with the "It's me" meditation. Yes—end on the soup message to her sister. Final line maybe: "There's soup." Or leave it hanging: "Anyway. There's soup." The word "anyway" echoing the mother's trailing-off habit. That's the ending.

Let me also consider the narrator's gender—implied female via "we were girls." Fine.

**The Number**

My mother has been dead for four years, and every month I pay the phone company forty-five dollars to keep her alive a little longer.

Autopay. I set it up the week after the funeral, when I found out the number would be released after ninety days of inactivity. Released, like an animal, like a bird. Somewhere out there her phone number would be given to a stranger, and some stranger's mother would answer when I called, and I could not allow that, so now the phone company has a standing arrangement with me: forty-five dollars a month, and in exchange, her number sits in their servers like a held breath, assigned to nobody, waiting.

Her greeting was nothing special. That's what I loved about it. "Hey, it's Ellen—leave it after the beep." Flat, a little rushed, the way she talked when she was doing something else, which was always. You can hear a cabinet close near the end. You can hear, very faintly, my father asking her a question from another room, six years before he died. [Father detail—nice, adds depth; keep brief.]

Some nights I call it. Not all nights. I scroll to E, thumb over the green, and usually that's enough—just to see it there, the same number I dialed when I was seven, stretching the kitchen cord down the hall and around the bathroom door for privacy. She ported the house line to a cell phone at sixty-eight because my brother nagged her into it, so the number in my phone and the number in my body are the same number. I know it the way I know my own hands.

Her voicemails were never about anything. "It's me. I made too much soup. Come by Sunday, or don't, but there's soup." She never said goodbye. She'd get to the end of the thought and just—hang up, mid-breath, like the machine couldn't hold her attention one second more. For years I found this rude. Now I would give anything to be dismissed by her again.

The last message is eleven seconds long. I have it backed up three times, on drives and in the cloud, in a file called mom—final.mp3, which is a terrible name but there it is. It's from a Tuesday in October, three days before the end. "Call me back. A pigeon's been coming to my fire escape and I think it likes me. That's all. Call me back." I did call back. I know I called back. But I couldn't tell you, now, what we said, and I never asked about the pigeon—not enough, not the right questions—and so the pigeon is hers. It's the one thing she took with her.

Here is what I did not know: the greeting was not mine. The messages were not mine. When you pay for a dead woman's phone number, you are renting a room in the phone company's building, and when you stop, they don't just reassign the number. They clear the room. Wipe the box. Everything I'd saved—the pigeon, the soup, my father's voice in the background of a greeting recorded in 2009—all of it lived on their servers, not in my phone, and in March, on a Tuesday night, because I was feeling strong, I let a payment lapse. One lapse. Forty-five dollars. [Wait—autopay wouldn't lapse. Better: the card expired. "The card on file expired and I didn't notice." Yes—more realistic and more painful: mundane cause.]

The card on file expired in February and I didn't notice the emails. In March, on a Tuesday night, because I'd had a good day and wanted to end it with her, I called, and a man's voice said, "You reached Des. You know what to do."

I sat down on the kitchen floor. Des. Young voice, unhurried, faintly amused, a man who has never once thought about his own mortality. His friends are in her voicemail box now. They leave messages about parties. I called every night that week just to hear the shape of it, the way you drive past your old house and stare at strangers' curtains.

I want to tell you I did something dignified. I didn't. I called and, after his beep, said: I'm sorry to do this to you. That number was my mother's for thirty-one years. She died four years ago and I kept paying for it so I could hear her say leave it after the beep. I don't need anything from you. Just—be nice to it. Then I hung up before he could ever hear me, which is not how it works, which means I hung up on myself.

Des never called back. He didn't have to. There was nothing to say.

Here is what I have instead. I have eleven seconds of pigeon. I have her syntax, which turns out to be unkillable. I start all my messages with it's me, as if there were only one me in the world, as if the person on the other end couldn't possibly have caller ID, as if the phone were still a bell ringing in an empty house and the voice on the line a mystery, a stranger calling out of the dark wanting to be found. I hang up without goodbyes. My brother says I've started doing the thing where I get to the end of a thought and just—

And Des's beep, when I still called, was the same beep. Beeps are universal. Some nights that was almost enough.

Last Sunday I made too much soup. I stood in my kitchen with a pot the size of a bathtub and understood, finally, what she had been doing all those years—not cooking, signaling. I called my sister and when she answered I said: It's me. I made too much soup. Come by, or don't.

But there's soup.
